analysis.title: US FOMC: why we favour a 25bp rate hike in October
key_insights: ANZ expects the FOMC to raise the fed funds target rate by 25bp to 4.0-4.25% at the 27-28 October meeting, a minority view against market pricing of a hold.
Market pricing implies about a 15% chance (3.7bp) of an October hike, which ANZ considers materially too low.
September CPI headline rose to 3.7% y/y from 3.4% and core rose to 2.6% y/y from 2.4%. Three-month annualised core CPI quickened to 3.4% from 2.0%, and six-month to 2.9% from 2.6%.
Supercore services inflation (ex-shelter) averaged 0.37% m/m in Q3 versus 0.17% in Q2. Core CPI goods rose 0.25% m/m in September, the fastest monthly pace since January 2025.
After the CPI and PPI releases, September core PCE is expected at 0.3% m/m (from 0.2%), implying 3.1% y/y versus 3.0% in August 2026 and 2.8% in September 2025.

Fed Chair Warsh set a standard at Jackson Hole that the FOMC must be confident underlying inflation is moving to target clearly and at sufficient speed. ANZ says September CPI did not provide that confidence.
Warsh gives no forward guidance, but ANZ judges him to lean hawkish and expects him to carry the committee if he thinks rates need to rise. A hike would boost his inflation-fighting credibility.
An October hike would fit the September median dot plot of two 25bp hikes this year and leave time to review data before the 8-9 December meeting.

Labour data should not deter the Fed: September payrolls rose a modest 29k, unemployment is 4.2%, the four-week average of initial claims is 198.5k (from 204k at the September FOMC), and the ADP four-week average is 18.5k.
Financial conditions are easy: the Chicago Fed NFCI is -0.50 versus -0.55 at the last FOMC and the 25-year average of -0.30. Warsh said he was hard pressed to call conditions restrictive.
The real fed funds rate is 0.3% on headline PCE and 0.7% on core PCE, below the NY Fed (1.0%) and Richmond Fed (1.85%) neutral estimates. ANZ puts real neutral at 1.0-1.50%.

ANZ sees little reason to depart from the usual practice of hiking at sequential meetings, noting the only exception in the last five tightening cycles was the hesitant 2015 liftoff from the zero lower bound.

ANZ previously expected a hold through the energy shock and AI build-out, but says that view no longer holds after the August and September inflation data. It does not see a post-pandemic-scale inflation problem, but sees sticky inflation with upside risks.
ANZ argues an October hike would speed the return to target, anchor inflation expectations and reduce the size of future hikes, and acknowledges the 3 November midterms.

macro_indicators.indicator: Chicago Fed National Financial Conditions Index
macro_indicators.interpretation: Slightly tighter than -0.55 at the last FOMC but still easier than the 25-year average of -0.30.
Below the NY Fed (1.0%) and Richmond Fed (1.85%) neutral estimates and ANZ's 1.0-1.50% estimate.

risk_factors: A hike could unsettle the AI-led investment boom and equity market, which solid growth depends on.
The trend decline in the real fed funds rate over the past 12 months may be leading to a misallocation of capital in the current boom.
Not raising rates could signal tolerance for inflation slippage and a policy framework based more on forecasts than data.
Sticky inflation with upside risks, and an energy shock.
The Fed may hold because of the proximity of the 3 November midterms, which ANZ acknowledges.
vol_and_positioning: Market pricing implies only about a 15% (3.7bp) probability of a hike at the 27-28 October FOMC.
High yield spread widening has stayed within recent sell-off ranges.
ANZ says the Fed may be wary of fanning market volatility and unsettling financing for the AI-led investment boom and stock market.
geopolitical: The report refers to a current energy shock affecting the inflation outlook.
US midterm elections on 3 November are acknowledged as a political backdrop, though the report says the Fed has been clear that they are not an obstacle to setting policy.
cross_bank_references: We agree with Chicago Fed president Goolsbee's assessment that the data were discouraging

tension_points.bull_case: Inflation is re-accelerating (core CPI 3-month annualised 3.4%, supercore 0.37% m/m in Q3) and the real fed funds rate of 0.3-0.7% is below neutral. A hike would restore Warsh's credibility and anchor inflation expectations, and fits the September dot plot of two hikes.
tension_points.bear_case: Market pricing implies only about a 15% chance of a hike. The Fed may fear unsettling the AI-led investment boom and equities, the midterms are on 3 November, and payrolls were only 29k.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence that underlying inflation is moving to target clearly and at sufficient speed, which September CPI did not show.

theme_stances.key_argument: September inflation data no longer show underlying disinflation, so an October hike would speed the return to target and anchor expectations.
theme_stances.evidence: We realise our view is a minority view
